chapter: Peano arithmetic: rules about whole numbers

sentences.text: Start with the whole numbers.
Zero, one, two, three, and so on.
Peano arithmetic is a precise system of rules about those numbers.
It tells us how the next number works, and how addition and multiplication behave.
It also gives us induction.
Imagine a row of dominoes.
Establish the first case, then show that whenever one case holds, the next one holds too.
Together, those two steps prove the property for every whole number.
We never have to check the numbers one at a time.
Arithmetic can also encode finite lists, fractions, and the steps of a calculation.
So this small starting point can express a surprising amount of mathematics.
Now give ourselves a larger framework.
Z F C is a standard collection of rules for set theory.
A set is a collection of mathematical objects.
The rules let us build new sets, work with infinite sets, and develop a great deal of ordinary mathematics.
Even the whole numbers can be built out of sets.
We can start with the empty set, then build a sequence representing zero, one, two, and so on.
Inside this framework we can also construct functions, real numbers, and spaces.
That is one reason Z F C is stronger than Peano arithmetic.
It can describe and justify much more than the arithmetic rules alone.
Why does the strength of the rules matter?
First, we need a word: consistency.
A consistent system never proves a contradiction, such as zero equals one.
Checking a particular proof is a finite task.
But saying that no proof of a contradiction exists is a statement about every possible proof.
There is a remarkable connection here.
A finite proof can itself be encoded as a whole number.
That lets arithmetic make statements about proofs.
In nineteen thirty one, Godel established his second incompleteness theorem.
Under its usual conditions, a consistent system with mechanically specified rules and enough arithmetic cannot prove its own formal consistency.
This applies to Peano arithmetic, and to Z F C.
So a system can check individual arguments without being able to establish, from its own rules, that those rules will never produce a contradiction.
A stronger system can sometimes provide that justification for a weaker one.
Here is how Z F C does it for Peano arithmetic.
It constructs the whole numbers, together with addition and multiplication, and checks that they satisfy the arithmetic axioms.
This is called building a model: a mathematical world where the rules hold.
Valid proof steps preserve truth in that world.
So an arithmetic proof cannot lead from those rules to a contradiction.
That gives a proof of the consistency of Peano arithmetic, carried out inside Z F C.
The justification depends on the stronger framework.
When Z F C asks about its own consistency, Godel's limit still applies.
Now repeat that idea one level higher.
Not all infinities have the same size.
An inaccessible cardinal is a special size of infinity with a useful feature for our story.
If one exists, the sets below it form a mathematical world satisfying Z F C.
So assuming such a cardinal exists gives us a way to prove that Z F C is consistent.
But we just met the obstacle.
If Z F C is consistent, it cannot prove its own consistency.
Therefore it cannot prove that an inaccessible cardinal exists, either.
If it could, the model we just described would supply the forbidden consistency proof.
Accepting an inaccessible cardinal is therefore an additional assumption beyond Z F C.
This is why reducing the assumptions behind a theorem is a meaningful mathematical goal.
We want to understand exactly how much of this larger framework the argument actually needs.

chapter: A finite witness inside a window
